note: Organises governance artifacts from team level to international level, helping an audit ask who is accountable at each layer.
title: AI governance: a systematic literature review

reading.body:
AI governance research is fragmented across five levels, from teams to international bodies, and no single framework fits every layer.

The review examined 28 studies and sorted governance artifacts into team, organization, industry, national, and international levels. It organized the analysis around four questions: who is responsible, what is managed, when oversight happens during development, and how it is carried out. The finding is that many frameworks exist but they are hard to compare and hard to match to a given situation.

For AI specifically, this matters because accountability is the part of governance that compute buildouts cannot supply on their own. A data center, a power contract, and a training run each sit inside some organization, and that organization sits inside an industry, a country, and a set of international arrangements. The review's contribution is a map of which artifacts live at which layer, which is what an audit needs before it can ask who answers for a decision.

What the data does not cover is equally clear. It reports a count of 28 studies and a citation count of 270, and nothing about which jurisdictions, sectors, or enforcement mechanisms were represented. It offers no evidence that any level's framework works, only that frameworks exist. The paper is a literature review, so it describes the state of governance research rather than the state of governance itself.

explain_beginner: This paper reviews existing research about how artificial intelligence is managed. The authors looked at 28 studies and grouped the ways people govern AI by level, from a small team up to international bodies. They also asked who is responsible, what parts of AI are controlled, when control happens during development, and how rules or tools are used. The main point is that many frameworks exist, but it is hard to compare them or pick one that fits. This matters because clearer governance can help organizations handle AI risks and know who should answer for decisions.
explain_business: For leaders, this review shows that AI oversight is not one single rulebook. The authors examined 28 studies and grouped governance approaches by level, from teams and organizations to industries, countries, and international bodies. They also mapped who carries responsibility, what is managed, when oversight should occur, and how it is delivered. In practice, this helps an executive see that AI governance spans multiple levels and cannot be handled with one generic approach. It informs decisions about assigning accountability at each layer, choosing suitable frameworks or tools, and checking whether current practices cover the full development cycle. It can guide a more coordinated governance plan.
explain_practitioner: The authors used a structured review method to study AI governance. They searched, selected, and examined 28 articles. Their analysis was organized around four questions: who carries responsibility, what parts are managed, when governance happens while AI systems are being built, and how it is carried out through different mechanisms. They then sorted governance artifacts into five levels: team, organization, industry, national, and international. The key result is a structured overview of existing solutions across these layers. This can help researchers identify gaps and propose more complete AI governance practices.
